suggested.question: Which issues should I fix first, and why?

answer.text: The two high-priority findings should be addressed first. The missing CloudTrail resource means no API activity in the account is being recorded, which is a direct gap in audit and incident-response capability required under HIPAA and FISMA. The access-log S3 bucket also lacks all four public-access block settings, meaning a single later ACL or policy change could expose Medicare PHI audit logs to the internet. Both are deterministic gaps with no ambiguity, and both carry direct regulatory consequences.

suggested.question: Explain "No aws_cloudtrail resource found in the submitted Terraform" for a non-technical stakeholder.

answer.text: Think of AWS CloudTrail as a security camera system for your cloud account. Every time someone — or any automated system — takes an action in your AWS environment (such as accessing data, changing a configuration, or creating a resource), CloudTrail records who did it, when, and from where. Without it, there is no activity log to review if something goes wrong.

citations.title: No aws_cloudtrail resource found in the submitted Terraform

answer.text: The review found that no CloudTrail recorder has been set up in the submitted infrastructure code. This means that right now, API activity across the account would not be captured for audit or incident response purposes. For a platform handling Medicare claims data — which is protected health information subject to HIPAA and federal FISMA rules — this is a significant gap, because both frameworks require a reliable audit trail of who accessed or changed sensitive data.

citations.title: No aws_cloudtrail resource found in the submitted Terraform

answer.text: HIPAA and FISMA both expect organisations to be able to demonstrate, after the fact, that PHI was accessed only by authorised parties. Without CloudTrail logs, the team would have no reliable way to investigate a potential breach, respond to a regulator's inquiry, or detect suspicious behaviour — such as an unexpected login or a configuration change that opened up access.

The recommended fix is straightforward: add a CloudTrail configuration that covers all regions and turns on log-file validation (a feature that proves the logs haven't been tampered with after the fact). This is a foundational control and is rated high priority in the review.

answer.text: The review found no aws_cloudtrail resource anywhere in the submitted Terraform. Without it, API activity in the account is not recorded beyond CloudTrail's default 90-day management-event history, leaving no durable audit trail for incident response or HIPAA/FISMA compliance.

answer.text: AWS Well-Architected guidance recommends establishing a trail per account (or an Organizations-level trail) and associating it with an S3 bucket. For longer retention and visibility of data events you should also attach a CloudWatch Logs log group. The review recommends enabling multi-region coverage and log-file validation so that tampering with log files is detectable.

suggested.question: Why not rely on CloudFront geo-restriction alone?

answer.text: The review explicitly considered CloudFront geo-restriction as an alternative to the WAF IP-allowlisting approach and rejected it for a straightforward reason: CloudFront is not confirmed to be in scope for this workload. Because there is no evidence in the submitted Terraform that CloudFront sits in front of these APIs, relying on its geo-restriction feature would mean depending on infrastructure that may not exist in the deployment.

citations.title: WAFv2 is deployed with IPv4 and IPv6 IP-set allowlisting and logging enabled, providing layer-7 access control aligned…

answer.text: Even if CloudFront were present, geo-restriction operates at the country level — it can block traffic originating from certain countries, but it cannot enforce the fine-grained partner IP allowlisting that this workload requires. The WAFv2 configuration, by contrast, uses explicit IPv4 and IPv6 IP-set rules to permit only known partner IP ranges, which is a much tighter control aligned with the partner-only access requirement.

citations.title: WAFv2 is deployed with IPv4 and IPv6 IP-set allowlisting and logging enabled, providing layer-7 access control aligned…

answer.text: The Well-Architected guidance also cautions against substituting coarser network controls for more capable ones. WAF provides layer-7 inspection — including rate limiting and rule sets — that geo-restriction simply cannot replicate. Geo-restriction alone would leave the APIs exposed to any traffic originating from within an allowed country, including malicious actors, rather than restricting access to the specific allowlisted partner addresses.
